blocks.text: A bar chart (or bar graph) is a graphical representation used to display categorical data with rectangular bars, where the length or height of each bar is proportional to the value it represents. Bar charts are used to compare quantities across distinct categories or groups. In biology, bar charts are valuable for showing data like the counts of different species, experimental groups, or measurement results from biological samples. The key characteristics of a bar chart are:

items: Categories are represented by the x-axis (horizontal axis).
Values or frequencies are represented by the y-axis (vertical axis).
Bars can be oriented vertically or horizontally.

blocks.text: Steps to create a bar chart with example
A team of research students conducted an insect diversity study in a local forest and counted the number of individuals for five common insect species over a month.

blocks.caption: Table: Relative abundance of the insect species

items: Purpose: To visually compare the abundance of five different insect species.
Categorical variable: Insect species (ladybug, ant, butterfly, bee, dragonfly).
Numerical variable: Number of individuals counted.

blocks.text: Greatest value is 120 (Ants). Scale the y-axis from 0 to 130 or 140. An increment of 10 or 20 is used for good readability. Let's choose 0 to 140 with increment of 20.

items: Draw a bar for ladybug up to 45 on the y-axis.
Draw a bar for ant up to 120 on the y-axis.
Draw a bar for butterfly up to 30 on the y-axis.
Draw a bar for bee up to 75 on the y-axis.
Draw a bar for dragonfly up to 20 on the y-axis.
Ensure bars are of equal width and evenly spaced.
Chart title: Insect species abundance in local forest

blocks.alt: Bar chart titled INSECT SPECIES ABUNDANCE IN LOCAL FOREST. Y-axis Number of individuals, 0 to 140 in steps of 20; x-axis Insect species. Five coloured bars: Ladybug 45 (16%), Ant 120 (41%), Butterfly 30 (10%), Bee 75 (26%), Dragonfly 20 (7%), with the percentage above each bar and a colour legend for all five species.
blocks.caption: Bar chart showing relative abundance of insect species in a local forest (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed bar chart titles its y-axis 'Abundance (%)', but the bars show counts and the book's own steps name the axis 'Number of individuals'; its legend also lists only three of the five species. The chart above uses 'Number of individuals' and a full legend.

A legend is a key or guide on a chart, graph, or map that explains the meaning of symbols, colours, patterns, or labels used in the visual. It helps the viewer understand what different elements represent, making the data or information easier to interpret and analyse. For example, in a bar chart with different colours for each category, the legend identifies what each colour corresponds to.
